sections.body: The AI Economist is the part of the atlas that looks at how artificial intelligence is used in economics and investing. In practice, that means models that forecast growth and inflation, systems that place and manage trades, tools that screen private deals, and software that scores credit risk. It also covers how portfolios are built, how market language is parsed, how alternative data is turned into signals, how agents carry out financial workflows, and how crypto markets are analysed. The work is not a single method. It mixes statistics, machine learning, natural language processing, optimisation, and data engineering. The common thread is decision making under uncertainty, where the data is noisy and the future is not fixed.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are mature. Forecasting pipelines, backtesting, text extraction, and risk dashboards run in production at many firms, and the site tracks 117 listed instruments tied to AI with daily prices as one visible slice of that activity. Other parts remain hard. Financial data is often short, non stationary, and shaped by the very models that try to predict it, so a model that works in one regime can fail in the next. Overfitting, look ahead bias, and unclear causality are persistent problems, and explainability is still limited when complex models drive decisions. Governance adds another constraint, because fiduciary duties, disclosure rules, and liability do not disappear when a model is involved. The honest limit is that AI can improve speed, coverage, and pattern detection, but it cannot remove uncertainty from markets or make economic cause and effect simple.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: Macroeconomic Econometrics and Fixed Income and Credit Risk cover the forecasting and lending side, where readers go for macro models, rate paths, default probabilities, and credit spreads. Quantitative Trading and Portfolio Construction sit closer to execution and allocation, covering signal design, transaction costs, risk budgeting, and the gap between a backtest and a live book. Private Equity and Deal Sourcing and Alternative Data address private markets and unusual inputs, including sourcing, diligence, web and satellite data, and the legal and ethical questions that come with them. Reading the Market's Language and Agent Workflows in Finance explain how text, filings, and news become structured signals, and how software agents chain tasks across research, compliance, and reporting. Crypto Markets and Decentralised Finance extends the same questions to digital assets and blockchain activity, while Governance and Fiduciary Risk gathers the rules, oversight duties, and accountability questions that cut across all ten areas, with the site holding 148 active AI lawsuits and 219 compliance and regulation pages as reference material.
